summary: Defines SIP extensions that let a caller express preferences about how a request is handled by servers. These include choosing which contact URIs the request is routed to and giving directives such as whether to try several places at once or one after another.

eli5.summary: When you call a family, you can say, "Ring the mobile first, not the home phone." This document is how a caller says it.

questions: what does accept-contact do in sip
what is the sip request-disposition header
how does a sip proxy rank contacts
subtitle: How a SIP caller can ask servers to route a call to the right device, or to handle it a certain way.

tldr.problem: SIP servers decide how to route a request using only the server administrator's policy and the callee's wishes. The caller has no way to say, for example, that it wants the work phone and not voicemail.
tldr.mechanism: Three new request header fields carry the caller's wishes: Accept-Contact and Reject-Contact choose among a callee's registered devices by their capabilities, and Request-Disposition asks servers to proxy or redirect, fork, recurse, and so on.
tldr.outcome: Proxies that own the target domain filter and rank the callee's contacts using these preferences, but they remain preferences, not guarantees. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 3841 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2004. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Callers Need a Say
sections.content:
When a SIP server receives a request, it makes several decisions: whether to proxy or redirect, which URIs to send it to, whether to fork, whether to search recursively, and whether to search in parallel or in sequence. Until this RFC, those choices came from the server's local policy, and the callee could shape them with a script such as one written in the Call Processing Language.

The caller had no voice. The RFC gives two examples: a caller who wants a particular person but only at work because it is a business call, and a caller who wants the person but not their voicemail. The extension is deliberately general purpose. It is a tool for building many services, one of which is a one number service where a single SIP URI covers a user's cell phone, PDA, work phone and home phone, and the caller picks the device from a menu.
sections.eli5: Normally the phone company decides which of your family's phones to ring. This lets the person calling say which phone they would like to try.

sections.title: Two Kinds of Preferences
sections.content:
The RFC defines two categories of caller preference. Request handling preferences live in the Request-Disposition header field and describe behavior wanted at a server, such as proxy versus redirect, or sequential versus parallel search. They can apply at every proxy or redirect server on the signaling path.

Feature preferences live in the Accept-Contact and Reject-Contact header fields. They contain feature sets, written with the same feature parameters that user agents use to describe their capabilities in RFC 3840. Accept-Contact describes agents the caller wants to reach. Reject-Contact describes agents that should not be used if they match.

Both can appear in any request, not only INVITE, but they only matter where a proxy has to pick a request target. If a proxy does not own the domain in the request URI, it never consults a location service and never gets to apply them. Mid-dialog requests are a typical case, since the routing was settled on the first request.
sections.eli5: There are two kinds of wishes. One is how the call should be handled, like try everyone at once. The other is which phone you want, like the mobile.

sections.title: Request-Disposition Directives
sections.content:
The value of Request-Disposition is a list of tokens, and there can be only one directive of each type per request. Servers SHOULD honor the directives. The compact form of the header is d.

  • proxy or redirect: whether each server proxies or redirects.
  • cancel or no-cancel: whether a proxy cancels other branches when a 200 OK arrives, or leaves that to the caller. With no-cancel a proxy still sends CANCEL on outstanding branches after a 6xx.
  • fork or no-fork: whether to try several addresses or only the best one, normally the one with the highest q-value.
  • recurse or no-recurse: whether a proxy follows addresses in a 3xx response or passes them upstream.
  • parallel or sequential: whether to try all addresses at once or one after another.
  • queue or no-queue: whether a temporarily unreachable callee should result in a queued call (answered with 182 Queued) or immediate rejection.

An example is Request-Disposition: proxy, recurse, parallel. The set of directives is not extensible on purpose, to avoid new SIP extensions being tunneled through this header. A user agent server SHOULD process the queue directive and MUST ignore the others.
sections.eli5: These are little instructions for the operator, like "connect me yourself" or "try all the numbers at the same time" or "put me on hold if they are busy."

sections.title: Accept-Contact and Reject-Contact
sections.content:
Each value of these headers is an asterisk followed by feature parameters. The asterisk only keeps the syntax in line with SIP extension guidelines. Compact forms are a for Accept-Contact and j for Reject-Contact. An example that asks for a mobile device is Accept-Contact: *;mobility="mobile";methods="INVITE".

A UAC is RECOMMENDED to include a sip.methods term (written just methods in the header) with the request method, and for SUBSCRIBE requests a sip.events term with the event package.

Accept-Contact values can carry two flags that decide how strict the match is:

  • require alone: a contact that does not match is not used, but a contact whose match is unknown still is. The proxy also prefers the best match among contacts of equal q-value.
  • explicit alone: all contacts are used, but one that is not an explicit match is tried last among contacts with the same q-value.
  • require and explicit together: only contacts that explicitly declared the feature set are used. Others are never tried, so the call fails unless a contact definitively matches.
  • neither: all contacts are used, non-matching ones last, and the best match first.

Preferences never override the callee's own ordering. They only choose among contacts with equal q-value. A UAC that wants to know whether servers understand the extension can add Proxy-Require: pref, and a 420 response means they do not.
sections.eli5: Accept-Contact says "I would love the mobile" and Reject-Contact says "not the voicemail." Extra words say how picky you are: just a hope, or the call must fail if there is no match.

sections.title: How a Proxy Matches and Ranks Contacts
sections.content:
A proxy applies this processing only if it owns the domain in the request URI and is using a location service that has capabilities for its targets. It may use any internal steps as long as results match those described, which are expressed through the feature set syntax of RFC 2533.

First the proxy extracts explicit preferences from Accept-Contact and Reject-Contact. Only if there are none does it infer implicit preferences: a required sip.methods term for the request method and, for subscriptions, a sip.events term for the Event header value. Each target URI gets a contact predicate built from the feature parameters in its registered Contact, plus its q-value (1.0 if none). A URI with no feature parameters is immune: it is set aside during matching and added back afterwards with a preference score of 1.0.

Then:

  • Reject-Contact predicates are applied first. A contact is discarded only if it explicitly declared the unwanted features.
  • For Accept-Contact, a non-matching predicate drops the contact if require is set, and otherwise is simply removed from that contact's matching set.
  • A score is computed for each remaining predicate: with N terms in the predicate, each matching feature tag adds 1/N, so scores range from zero to one.
  • If explicit is set and the score is below one, the contact is dropped when require is also set, or its score becomes zero when not.
  • The overall caller preference Qa is the arithmetic average of the scores.

Finally, contacts are sorted by the callee's q-value, grouped into equivalence classes of equal q-value, and ordered by Qa inside each class. If implicit preferences removed every target, the proxy reverts to the original target set, so the caller sees a useful 405 or 489 instead of an unexplained 480. With explicit preferences an empty set produces a 480, and the RFC chooses not to report the callee's capabilities because that could leak sensitive information. A redirect server must not include feature parameters in the contacts it returns, so the preferences are not applied twice.
sections.eli5: The proxy is like a receptionist with a list of phones. First she crosses out the ones you said no to, then she gives each remaining phone points for how well it fits your wishes, and rings the best fit first. She never skips ahead of the order the person you are calling asked for.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC walks through five registered contacts, u1 to u5, and an INVITE with a Reject-Contact for actor="msg-taker" with video, plus three Accept-Contact values (audio with require, video with explicit, and methods BYE with class business).

The outcome is as follows. u5 has no feature parameters, so it is immune. u3 is the only contact that explicitly declared video and being a message taker, so the Reject-Contact discards it. u2 fails the first Accept-Contact, which has require, so it is dropped. That leaves u1 and u4, with Qa of 0.83 and 0.5. After sorting by q-value, the final order is u5 (q 0.5), then u1, then u4 (both q 0.2, ordered by Qa).
sections.eli5: Five phones, three wishes. The proxy crosses off the ones that break your rules, scores the rest, and rings them best first. The phone with no label is always allowed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Caller preferences change how a request is handled, so requests that carry them SHOULD be integrity-protected with the sips mechanism from RFC 3261 section 26. A proxy may add preference headers as if it were a UAC, but MUST NOT modify or remove an existing value, which matters when S/MIME signatures cover those headers.

Matching needs set operations and searches, which gives an attacker a way to send requests stuffed with preferences to overload a server. Servers SHOULD reject requests with too many rules, and the RFC says a reasonable limit is around 20.
sections.eli5: Someone could write a giant wish list just to keep the receptionist busy. So the receptionist may say no to lists that are far too long.

items.label: cancel-directive
items.desc: Proxy cancels other branches after a 2xx, or leaves it to the caller.

items.label: fork-directive
items.desc: Try several addresses, or only the best one.

items.label: recurse-directive
items.desc: Follow 3xx addresses, or forward them upstream.

items.label: parallel-directive
items.desc: All addresses at once, or one at a time.

items.label: queue-directive
items.desc: Queue the call (182 Queued) or reject immediately.

viz.caption: WHAT HAPPENS TO A NON-MATCHING CONTACT

cells: Never tried; call fails unless a contact explicitly matches
Dropped if it does not match; still used if match is unknown
Tried last among contacts with the same q-value
Tried last; best match is tried first
